questions.q: A screenwriter's film about a factory disaster gives the victims no lives beyond their suffering, so the audience will feel moved and outraged. What would Baldwin's "Everybody's Protest Novel" say?
choices: It needs a clearer inciting incident
It reduces people to a category, denying their full humanity, and so fails as art and as protest
It should cut the victims' scenes and focus on the investigators
It breaks the unity of action
questions.explain: Baldwin argued that protest fiction which turns people into symbols of a cause rejects their beauty, dread and power, and so fails on its own terms.

questions.q: In Baldwin's view, what is wrong with sentimentality?
choices: It is a parade of excessive, false feeling that lets readers feel virtuous without facing a real person
It slows the pace of the second act
It breaks the contract between writer and reader by being too difficult
It shows rather than tells
questions.explain: Baldwin called sentimentality a mark of dishonesty: readers enjoy their own compassion instead of meeting a complicated human being.

questions.q: A columnist wants to write about her brother's arrest during a week of protests in her city. Which approach is closest to the title essay of *Notes of a Native Son*?
choices: Lead with the most newsworthy fact and add context in descending order
Write only about the protests, leaving her family out to stay objective
Braid the family story with the public events so each explains the other, and end on an argument the story has earned
Find the resolution first, then build complications toward it
questions.explain: Baldwin braided his father's death and funeral with the 1943 Harlem riot, so private and public anger illuminate each other.

questions.q: A reporter is asked to explain 'what the community thinks' about a police shooting. What distinction from Baldwin is useful here?
choices: Situation versus story
Contract versus Status
Showing versus telling
Spokesman versus witness: report what you have seen and heard rather than presuming to speak for everyone
questions.explain: In a 1984 interview with Julius Lester, Baldwin said a spokesman presumes to speak for others; he saw himself as a witness.

questions.q: Writing *Blues for Mister Charlie*, a play based loosely on the murder of Emmett Till, what did Baldwin say he feared?
choices: That he could never draw a valid portrait of the murderer
That the audience would find the trial scenes too long
That the play had no clear protagonist
That Broadway would not accept a split set
questions.explain: In his preface he said his fear was failing to make the murderer a valid portrait, which is the protest-novel argument applied to the villain.

questions.q: According to Baldwin's 1984 Paris Review interview, what is the hardest thing to achieve in rewriting?
choices: A strong midpoint reversal
Simplicity, because it means stripping away disguises you didn't know you had
An ending that is surprising yet inevitable
Cutting every adverb
questions.explain: Baldwin said simplicity is hardest, and that the goal is a sentence as clean as a bone.

questions.q: In "The Creative Process" (1962), what does Baldwin say marks the artist out from most people?
choices: A mastery of the three-act structure
A duty to entertain before instructing
The need to cultivate the state of being alone, which most people avoid, and report back what society would rather not know
Loyalty to a movement or cause
questions.explain: Baldwin argued that the artist's solitude lets them tell society truths it resists, which is why societies battle the artist as a disturber of the peace.

ideas: Protest fiction fails when it insists that a person's social category is the only thing about them that is real.
Sentimentality is a display of excessive, false feeling and a mark of dishonesty, not of compassion.
A writer should be a witness to what they have seen, not a spokesman who presumes to speak for others.
Societies have always battled the artist as an incorrigible disturber of the peace.
